## What the model says

A multinomial processing tree (MPT; [Batchelder & Riefer, 1999](https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03210812))
describes a response as the end of a path through discrete states. This tree is written for cued
recall of a list item from a set of candidates, the task of the [M3 simple-span page](m3.qmd). With
probability `Pi` the cued item is in memory. Given that, with probability `Pb` its position is
retrieved too, and the response is correct. It uses the two memory states of the binding model of
[Oberauer (2019)](https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.86) in the reverse order. In Oberauer's tree, which
the [MPT article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_mpt.html) uses to introduce covariates, the
binding is tested first: its `Pb` is the probability of retrieving the binding on any trial, and its
`Pi` the probability of item memory on trials where the binding was not retrieved. Here `Pi` holds
for every trial and `Pb` only for trials with the item in memory, the order of the article's
real-data example. With that tree's guessing rates set from the same response set, `GcorrPi`
$= 1/(1 + n_\text{other})$, `GcorrNoPi` $= 1/N$ and `GotherNoPi`
$= n_\text{other}/(n_\text{other} + n_\text{npl})$ (the share of list items among the wrong
candidates; with no wrong candidate on the screen `GcorrNoPi` is 1 and `GotherNoPi` multiplies
$1 - 1 = 0$, so any value in [0, 1] will do), the two trees give the same likelihood under a change
of parameters: that tree's `Pb` is $P_i P_b$, and its `Pi` is $P_i (1 - P_b) / (1 - P_i P_b)$. An
item in memory without its position leaves a guess among the $1 + n_\text{other}$ list items on the
screen, the correct one among them; an item not in memory leaves a guess among all $N$ candidates. With $n_\text{other}$
other list items and $n_\text{npl}$ lures, $N = 1 + n_\text{other} + n_\text{npl}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\text{corr}) &= P_i P_b + P_i (1 - P_b) \tfrac{1}{1 + n_\text{other}} + (1 - P_i) \tfrac{1}{N} \\
P(\text{other}) &= P_i (1 - P_b) \tfrac{n_\text{other}}{1 + n_\text{other}} + (1 - P_i) \tfrac{n_\text{other}}{N} \\
P(\text{npl}) &= (1 - P_i) \tfrac{n_\text{npl}}{N}
\end{aligned}
$$

`Pi` and `Pb` are estimated. The five guessing rates, the fractions in these formulas, are fixed by
the response set: `gl_corr` $= 1/(1 + n_\text{other})$ and `gl_other` $= n_\text{other}/(1 + n_\text{other})$
for the guess among list items, `g_corr` $= 1/N$, `g_other` $= n_\text{other}/N$ and `g_npl`
$= n_\text{npl}/N$ for the guess among all candidates. They enter bmm's `mpt()` as covariates, data
columns that the branch expressions use.

## The task

One trial is the cued recall of the [M3 page](m3.qmd): a list of letters is studied, one position is
cued, and the participant picks the letter that was there from candidates on the screen: the correct
letter, `n_other` other list letters and `n_npl` letters that were not on the list. The counts enter
the likelihood through the guessing rates only. Set size limits `n_other` (at most set size − 1) and
does not enter otherwise.

## Explore

The tree shows each state and each branch with its current probability: a parameter, or a guessing
rate written as the share of the candidates guessed among (1/5: the correct letter among five list
letters). An edge is drawn as wide
as the probability that a trial passes along it, and each leaf shows the probability of that path;
the paths ending in one category add up to its bar. Raising `Pi` moves weight from the guess among all
candidates to the list; raising `Pb` moves it from the guess among list items to a correct response.

bmm estimates `Pi` and `Pb` on the logit scale with a logistic(0, 1) prior, whose SD is π/√3 ≈ 1.81.
Each slider spans the prior mean ± 3 SD on that scale, so `Pi` and `Pb` run from 0.004 to 0.996 and start at the prior
mean, 0.5 (dashed bars).

## Across task settings

The guessing rates follow from the counts, so the tree predicts the response-set effect without a new
parameter, and it predicts a floor: a trial on which the position is retrieved is correct whatever
else is on the screen. Lures enter only through the guess among all candidates, so adding lures moves
P(correct) toward $P_i P_b + P_i (1 - P_b) / (1 + n_\text{other})$, not toward 0.

The [M3](m3.qmd) describes the same task with activations instead of states: every candidate gets
background activation `b`, list items add general activation `a`, the cued item adds context
activation `c`, and under the simple rule a category's probability is its share of the summed
activation $S$. With these additive activations the M3 is the same likelihood as this tree for any
one response set. With $b = 0.1$ and $S = (b + a + c) + n_\text{other} (b + a) + n_\text{npl}\, b$, the summed
activation,

$$
P_i = \frac{(1 + n_\text{other})\, a + c}{S}, \qquad P_b = \frac{c}{(1 + n_\text{other})\, a + c}.
$$

This mapping depends on the counts. Holding `Pi` and `Pb` fixed across response sets (solid lines) is
therefore a different prediction from holding `a` and `c` fixed (dotted lines): the lines meet at the
circle and part away from it.

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="mpt-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="mpt-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/mpt.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `mpt_tree()` writes the tree as one branch expression per response
category, `mpt()` turns it into a model and declares the guessing rates as covariates, `dmpt()` returns
the log probability of a set of response counts, and `bmm()` estimates `Pi` and `Pb` from data;
`my_data` stands for your own data, with the five rates as columns, and fitting runs Stan through
brms. See the [MPT article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_mpt.html), which fits this kind of
tree to the data of the M3 article, and the reference pages for
[`mpt_tree()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/mpt_tree.html),
[`mpt()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/mpt.html) and
[`dmpt()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/mptdist.html).
